t: States Offer Perks To Attract Healthcare Workers to Rural Areas — With a Catch

p: LĪHUʻE, Hawaiʻi — Dylan Lawton realized something was wrong when he struggled to use his right leg to hit the brakes while driving.

Within a matter of hours, scans showed the third-year medical student had a brain tumor. But the island of Kauaʻi, where he was completing his clinical rotation, has no neurosurgeons. So Lawton was medically evacuated on a plane to Straub Benioff Medical Center on O‘ahu, Hawaiʻi’s most populous island. There, the then-27-year-old was diagnosed with a type of lung cancer commonly found in nonsmokers, which was stage 4 and had spread to his brain.

Lawton said he wasn’t surprised by the extent of the healthcare shortages on Kauaʻi. Although he’s from Oʻahu, he grew up aware that his uncle on Kauaʻi needed to travel off-island to receive cancer treatment. It was one reason Lawton chose to participate in the University of Hawaiʻi medical school program that trains students on rural Kauaʻi, his grandparents’ home island. The cost of medical school is covered if the students practice medicine for four years on Kauaʻi after completing their residency. But now he needs ongoing, specialized treatment in a place with limited resources and only one full-time oncologist, who practices outside the hospital system where Lawton receives his treatment.
“I am experiencing the very thing that I was brought to fix,” Lawton said. “It crosses my mind all the time.”

“The requirement might be a pretty big one compared to the level of award that that individual is receiving, no matter what the degree is,” she said.

For example, Michigan is offering scholarships to students training to be emergency medical service professionals. But even though less training is required to become an EMT, those students will be held to the same five-year service commitment as physicians.

The retention rate of clinicians who continue to work in health professional shortage areas continues to drop in years two and three after they complete service obligations.
The Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services, which oversees the Rural Health Transformation Program, declined to comment on the record about the five-year service requirement.

, a professor at the University of North Carolina School of Medicine who studies workforce incentive programs for physicians, pointed to two provisions in the Rural Health Transformation Program service requirements that allow for flexibility. One allows participants to move around the state throughout their service as long as they continue to practice in rural areas. The other largely leaves it to states to create the incentive programs in whatever way suits their needs, outside of the five-year service commitment.
“There’s not any heavy hand in federal requirements with this,” Pathman said, adding that the flexibility may come with some risk. “We’re hoping 50 states get this right.”

of the Rural Health Transformation Program. Over 100 million people nationwide live in areas with a health professional shortage, according to the federal Health Resources and Services Administration. And rural areas represent 62% of the places with a shortage of primary care professionals.

The state is using some of its Rural Health Transformation Program funds on recruitment and retention initiatives that expand on established programs, such as the Kauaʻi Medical Training Track, which is funded by Facebook founder Mark Zuckerberg and wife Priscilla Chan, a trained pediatrician, who own an estate on the island.

With the new federal funds, the state will provide up to $200,000 each to select healthcare workers who agree to practice in a rural area of Hawaiʻi for at least five years. Some of those providers could practice on Kauaʻi, adding to the medical base created through the Chan-Zuckerberg funding.

The Kauaʻi Medical Training Track, run by the University of Hawai‘i, is still in its early phases. The first cohort of students recently graduated and started residencies this summer, so the program awaits its first returning doctors. Kaua‘i has only one residency option, family medicine, which started this year.

, who runs the Kaua‘i training track program, has been focused on building a community of providers and patients the students will feel connected to when they return to Kauaʻi to fulfill the program’s service commitment after their residency. While studying on Kauaʻi, the students live in a house in a residential neighborhood, and the university ships their vehicles to the island from Oʻahu. They are mentored by clinicians who will become their colleagues, and they treat patients they may see again when they return.

“These are not just medical students who are going to be doctors. These are going to be community members on the island,” Hong said. “Getting that experience early on is really important to get those seeds planted.”

p: that having community ties to rural areas is important for retaining physicians. Physicians’ feeling integrated in a community resulted in higher anticipated retention.

But for Lawton, it’s not clear what will happen to his four-year service commitment to work on Kaua‘i. While on Oʻahu last year, he was able to get the brain surgery he needed. He took a year off medical school to go through 13 cycles of chemotherapy. He’s in remission now and resumed his final year of school.
Because Lawton’s cancer is incurable, he will need to continue receiving cancer treatment on Oʻahu or elsewhere. He needs to see his doctor monthly.

Lawton said he’s working with the medical school to see what options would be available to him when he finishes his residency so he can fulfill his service requirement on Kauaʻi. He just submitted residency applications for internal medicine, a training specialty that isn’t an option on Kaua‘i.
“No matter what happens,” Lawton said, “I’ll try my best to stay here as much as I can.”
